title: Non-lodging funds create tax gap
full_text:
The SMSF sector has a small but growing gap in the non-payment of income tax, a situation strongly linked to non-lodging funds.
The ATO has flagged the shortfall in the amount of tax it expects to receive from the SMSF sector has grown in line with the increase in the number of funds that fail to lodge an annual return, with more than $100 million owing for the 2024 financial year.
The regulator released the figures as part of a wider report on tax gap estimates for that income year across a range of sectors it oversees, with the analysis showing the difference between what it expects to collect and the amount that would have been collected if every taxpayer was compliant with relevant tax law.
For 2023/24, the ATO estimated the total net tax gap was $72.7 billion, or 10.3 per cent of the total theoretical tax of $707 billion, and small business income tax, individual income tax, and goods and services tax gaps accounted for $59.7 billion, or more than 82 per cent of the total tax gap.
By comparison, the small super funds sector, which included 531,000 SMSFs and 940 small Australian Prudential Regulation Authority (APRA)-regulated funds, had a gap of 4.1 per cent, or $104 million, indicating the ATO collected just under 96 per cent of the $2.54 billion income tax payable by those funds for that year.
Statistics released with the estimate figures show the gap for the previous year, 2022/23, was 3.7 per cent, for 2021/22 it was 3.8 per cent, marking a small increase from 3.3 per cent in 2020/21 but a relatively larger rise from 2.1 per cent in 2019/20, which is consistent with changes in the number of non-lodging funds.
“The non-lodging population contributes to the gap with the total funds not lodging a SMSF annual return (SAR) increasing each tax year,” the ATO stated.
In its report, the ATO highlighted that since 2018, the number of funds not lodging an SAR was only 812, or 0.15 per cent of registered SMSFs, but that figure had climbed to 65,566, or 10.8 per cent of registered funds, in line with the tax gap estimate.
It acknowledged the difficulty in calculating this figure for the small super fund sector, but noted it was a tool it could use for further compliance action.
“Our estimates do not account for differences where there are alternative views on tax law interpretation. In these circumstances, differences can exist between reasonably arguable positions presented by us and taxpayers,” it stated.
“The gap estimate is a lagging measure as compliance results take several years to flow through. This is due to the complexity of the market and the elapsed time associated with finalising our compliance activities.
“As the nation’s principal tax collector, we use tax gap estimates to inform strategies to improve tax compliance over time. We engage with a range of stakeholders to understand risks and drivers, and how we can collaborate to maximise voluntary compliance.”
author: Jason Spits
heading: Superannuation and Investments
